hints: Think about the size of glycine. It has the smallest possible R group, just one hydrogen atom, so where must it be to let three helices pack very tightly?
Remember which amino acid can make disulfide bonds, and what type of bond actually holds the three collagen strands together.
walkthrough:
**Recall why glycine is so special in collagen**

Glycine is the smallest amino acid. Its R group is just $H$.

In collagen, every third amino acid is glycine. That tiny size is what lets the three polypeptides wind so closely together.

**Check the first statement about position**

The statement says glycine is on the outside of the helices. That is backwards.

Glycine must be on the inside, facing the centre of the triple helix, exactly because it is so small. An outside position would not help packing, so this described feature does not contribute.

**Check the second statement about bonding**

The statement says disulfide bonds form between glycines. This is impossible for two reasons.

First, only cysteine (with sulfur in its R group) can form disulfide bonds, not glycine. Second, collagen strands are joined by hydrogen bonds, not disulfide bonds. So this described feature also does not contribute.

Both statements are incorrect descriptions, so the correct row is X and X.

options.A: Incorrect, as both descriptions are wrong. Glycine is inside not outside, and no disulfide bonds form between glycines in collagen.
options.B: Incorrect, as the first description is wrong. Glycine lines the inside of the triple helix to allow close packing, not the outside.
options.C: Incorrect, as the second description is wrong. Collagen is stabilised by hydrogen bonds, and glycine cannot form disulfide bonds.
options.D: Correct, as neither description contributes. Glycine is on the inside, and collagen has no glycine to glycine disulfide bonds.
